transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Lena (Peregrine CTO), Ravi (Peregrine ML Infra), Priya (Peregrine SRE)
---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we scheduled a deep-dive on GPU runtime profiling, TensorRT-LLM vs v L L M, and CUDA graphs — wanna make sure this is the right scope, Lena?
[00:15] Lena (Peregrine CTO): Yeah that's right, we're seeing variance in p95 latency when we move from our local vLLM experiments to the cloud TensorRT tests. goal is to understand why and what tradeoffs there are for KV cache and batching.
[00:30] Ethan (Redwood SE): Great, we'll walk through the profiling captures we ran against your sample model (7B), also a 13B run for peak throughput. we'll show kernel selection differences, where tensorrt-llm picks faster fused kernels and where vllm has different memory traffic patterns.
[00:45] Ravi (Peregrine ML Infra): Quick note, our production seq len distribution is weird — 70% short (<512) and 30% long (~4k) so the warm KV cache behavior matters a lot.
[01:05] Sofia (Redwood SE): good to call that out — batching strategy needs to be adaptive. static batch size gives great throughput for short seqs but blows up latency for the long ones.
[01:22] Priya (Peregrine SRE): also fyi we have strict VPC egress rules and KMS restrictions, so any test infra must go through our peered VPC or we use the customer-managed KMS for keys.
[01:40] Maya: noted, we'll include VPC checklist. okay Ethan can you take us through the first profile?
[01:48] Ethan: sure, starting with the vLLM baseline — this was a 7B offline run on an A100-80GB. we see steady p50 around 40ms for short prompts, but p95 spikes to 420ms when there's KV cache misses on long-context requests because vllm streams kv updates differently. the kernel timeline shows heavy small-gemm kernels and a lot of memory ops.
[02:18] Lena: when you say small-gemm do you mean the attention matmul split into many small kernels? that's what we suspected.
[02:28] Ethan: yes exactly, vllm does more granular attention kernels which can be more efficient in some regimes but increases kernel launch overhead and adds to scheduler jitter.
[02:40] [02:40] Speaker 1: (mumbling) we saw similar in our internal runs, yeah
[02:45] Ethan: Contrast that with TensorRT-LLM — the tensorrt build fuses multiple ops into fewer kernels and uses cuBLAS/cuSparse fused paths when quantized int8 is active. that reduces kernel launches but increases sustained GPU utilization; so on short requests p50 improved to ~28ms but cold p95 on long sequences depends on how the KV cache is warmed and on whether CUDA Graphs are used.
[03:12] Ravi: tell me more on CUDA Graphs — we tried enabling them but saw occasional hangs and had to restart the process. is that expected?
[03:20] Ethan: there is nuance — CUDA Graphs give great latency stability by capturing the launch pattern and replaying but they are sensitive to dynamic shapes. if your workload has variable seq lengths (which you do) graphs can be brittle unless you use sequence bucketing or capture multiple graphs for canonical shapes. we saw a mismatch on dynamic KV cache sizes causing graph replay assertions in our early tests.
[03:52] Maya: and that explains Priya's stability observation. Priya, were the hangs reproducible or intermittent?
[04:00] Priya: intermittent — maybe once every few hours under heavy load. It wasn't a hard crash, more like a long stall where p95 shoots up to several seconds.
[04:10] Ethan: that aligns with what we saw: graph capture + eviction + async IO interplay can produce stalls. recommended pattern: capture graphs for the common seqlen buckets (e.g., 64, 512, 2048, 4096) and provide a light-weight fallback path that doesn't use graphs for outliers.
[04:34] Lena: how big an engineering lift is that for us? we don't want to maintain lots of graphs.
[04:42] Ethan: depends on model and traffic. buckets reduce number of graphs; also Redwood runtime can automate capture for the top N shapes and fallback when mismatch detected. we can show you our auto-capture heuristics in the deck.
[05:00] Sofia: also quantization plays into this — INT8 kernels in TensorRT often rely on different fused kernels; memory layout changes can affect KV cache hits and alignment. for example we saw 1.3x throughput with int8 on 7B but sequence-level variance increased for long sequences.
[05:22] Ravi: did you compare accuracy/regression when you quantized? we can't sacrifice our early-generation hallucination rates.
[05:30] Ethan: yes we ran evals on the dev prompts — minimal accuracy regression at per-token perplexity and downstream NLU tests for int8 with calibration. but it's model dependent; we recommended running an eval suite you own.
[05:48] Maya: can you talk about kernel selection heuristics — when does the runtime pick cuBLAS vs custom fused attention?
[05:56] Ethan: runtime measures matrix dims, sequence length, and available scratch memory. for wide matrices and shorter sequences cuBLAS matmul paths win; for long-sequence fused attention with optimized memory reuse and fused softmax we pick custom kernels. the selection also depends on quantization type — int8 path will prefer tensor cores and grouped ops.
[06:20] [06:20] Speaker 2: (background) we pushed a new patch last night that improved kernel selection heuristics
[06:25] Ethan: right, that patch adjusts the threshold for switching to fused attention based on occupancy estimations. it helps p95 on mid-range sequences (512-1024).
[06:35] Lena: ok about KV cache — our concern is memory pressure when many concurrent users keep large caches; we saw OOMs on smaller instances. any quick wins?
[06:48] Sofia: a few patterns — shard KV cache across GPUs (horizontal sharding) if you have multi-GPU nodes, use soft eviction policies (LRU-ish) and prefer prefix caching for common prompts. Redwood runtime also supports cache warmers for known sequences so cold-starts are less severe.
[07:08] Ravi: we run on single-GPU pods now for autoscaling; would you recommend multi-GPU?
[07:14] Ethan: depends on throughput needs. multi-GPU helps when model or cache doesn't fit single device memory or when you want horizontal throughput scaling. but it adds network overhead for KV exchange. For your mix (70% short, 30% long) a hybrid: keep some dedicated multi-gpu pools for long-context heavy flows and single-GPU for short-flows. Redwood routing can split traffic by policy.
[07:38] Priya: what about VPC and on-prem — if we want private deployment can we run these TensorRT kernels in our air-gapped infra?
[07:46] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem runtime. we provide a private control plane and can ship the runtime images. for KMS you can plug in an HSM or customer-managed KMS. note that some vendor binaries (e.g., certain TensorRT plugins) require compatible driver stacks — we'll document exact driver/kernel versions in the security pack.
[08:12] Lena: good. back to benchmarks — can you walk me through the latency vs throughput tradeoff you found between tensorrt-llm and vllm?
[08:20] Ethan: summarized: for short seqs tensorrt-llm wins both p50 and p95 due to fused kernels and tensor cores, often ~25-35% lower latency. for long sequences vllm's streaming approach sometimes wins on memory usage, which can translate to higher sustained throughput on constrained memory instances. but when we enable int8 + CUDA graphs with TensorRT, throughput at tail improves and can surpass vllm if graphs are stable.
[08:56] Ravi: when you say streaming approach for vllm that reduces memory, is that because it evicts intermediate KV or uses recomputation?
[09:03] Ethan: primarily more on-the-fly recompute and different checkpointing strategy, plus chunked attention windows for very long contexts. it trades compute for memory which helps in small-GPU scenarios.
[09:18] Maya: here's a question we get a lot — how to choose between dedicated vs hosted for a team like Peregrine?
[09:26] Sofia: hosted is fastest to get started; dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput and isolation. Private on-prem is for compliance or strict residency. for Peregrine, if you want to keep KMS in-house and avoid egress rules, Private or Dedicated with VPC peering are the options.
[09:50] Marcus (Platform Eng): if we go Private, do we lose Redwood's auto-graph capture / kernel updates? how do we stay patched?
[09:58] Ethan: Redwood Private ships with the same runtime; we support upgrades via your release window. auto-capture is part of the runtime but the capture logs are stored locally under your control unless you opt-in for Redwood-managed telemetry.
[10:18] Lena: are there memory layout changes we should be worried about when switching quantization and kernels? i.e., could alignment change cause more cache misses?
[10:26] Sofia: yes, int8 packing changes layout; fused kernels may use different tensor strides. in some cases you might see small regression in KV lookup micro-patterns; we usually recommend smoke tests on representative workloads.
[10:42] [10:42] Speaker 3: (background) will add note about memory stride check
[10:45] Ethan: one more practical tip — throttle batch sizes for long sequences. Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching with per-model rules: max_tokens_per_batch and timeouts per bucket. that keeps latency SLO for interactive flows.
[11:05] Ravi: could you share the exact flags you used for TensorRT-LLM runs?
[11:10] Ethan: sure: --tensorrt-engine=int8_calib_v2, --cuda-graphs=enabled, --graph-buckets=64,512,2048,4096, --kv-shard=auto, --batching=max_tokens=4096,timeout_ms=12. we'll paste full command in the deck.
[11:34] Priya: that timeout seems low, do you recommend 12ms for our traffic?
[11:38] Ethan: it's aggressive for high qps short flows; adjust per bucket. the idea is to cap wait time so short requests don't get stuck behind big batches.
[11:50] Lena: any experiments on mixed-precision (FP16) vs int8?
[11:55] Sofia: fp16 is safer accuracy-wise and still gives tensor-core speedups; int8 wins more on cost but needs calibration. many customers start with fp16 then pilot int8 on non-critical routes.
[12:08] Maya: ok let's talk about metrics you'll need to share for our internal benchmark: what should we collect?
[12:15] Ethan: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput, GPU util, SM efficiency, PCIe bandwidth, kernel launch counts, CUDA graph replay stats, KV cache hit/miss ratio, memory highwater, and per-request token counts. also store example request ids for tail cases.
[12:42] Ravi: we can provide the logs, but will need instructions for sensitive info redaction.
[12:48] Maya: we'll provide a scrub script and a checklist for redaction before you upload.
[12:56] [12:56] Speaker 1: cool
[12:58] Ethan: a couple more gotchas — watch out for asynchronous IO thresholds; if the NVMe staging is slow it can cascade into long stalls during graph replay. also PCIe topology can matter if you're sharding KV between GPUs.
[13:20] Priya: for our on-prem nodes, we have NVLink disabled on some racks. does that materially change recommended topology?
[13:28] Ethan: yes, without NVLink you see increased PCIe traffic and latency for KV exchange; prefer single-GPU for flows that can't tolerate cross-GPU jitter. If you need multi-GPU, ensure NVLink or RDMA is available.
[13:46] Lena: any suggestions for canarying a migration from vLLM to TensorRT-LLM?
[13:52] Sofia: start with a small percent of traffic on non-critical endpoints, run A/B with the same prompts and compare p95/p99 and throughput. run the eval suite for accuracy regressions. also stage CUDA graphs in a separate rollout so you can switch them off quickly.
[14:12] Maya: alright let's go through rough timeline: Maya to send deck by 11/20, Peregrine provides sample prompts and creds by 11/22, Redwood to run controlled benchmarks and send results by 11/26, then decision meeting week of 11/29.
[14:32] Lena: sounds good. any other blockers?
[14:36] Ravi: we need the exact driver and container versions for compliance review.
[14:41] Ethan: we'll include driver/kernel matrix in the packet.
[14:45] Priya: and include KMS/HSM integration docs please.
[14:48] Maya: will do. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the recap email with links.
[14:55] [14:55] End of recording
